goal:
Make `slugify` in `src/slugify.js` turn Latin letters with diacritics into plain ASCII: `slugify("Crème Brûlée")` returns `"creme-brulee"` and `slugify("Łódź")` returns `"lodz"`.

This covers every Latin letter, not only those Unicode can split into a base letter and an accent: letters with a stroke and ligatures take their usual ASCII spelling (for example `ø` → `o`, `æ` → `ae`, `ß` → `ss`). Accents count whether the title writes them precomposed or as separate combining marks after the letter.

Keep everything that works today. In particular, letters of other scripts stay exactly as they are: `slugify` keeps Cyrillic, Greek, Japanese, and every other script unchanged, apart from lower case.

constraints: Change as few files as possible.
Delete or simplify existing code before you add code.
Write a failing test that reproduces the problem before you change any source file.

+ * Turns a title into a URL slug: Latin letters use ASCII spellings, lower case,

 export function slugify(title) {

candidates.approach: Add a Latin-only folding stage inside src/slugify.js before the existing separator cleanup. Decompose Latin base letters with NFD, remove their attached combining accents, and use an explicit, reviewed mapping for Latin letters that decomposition does not handle, including strokes and ligatures such as ł, ø, æ, and ß. Handle already-decomposed accents in the same Latin context. Do not normalize the entire title: leave non-Latin portions to the existing lowercase-and-cleanup pipeline. This combines Unicode’s accent coverage with an exception inventory covering the remaining Latin letters.
candidates.firstStep: Add regression tests for the two requested examples, precomposed versus decomposed Latin accents, stroke letters and ligatures, and unchanged Cyrillic, Greek, Japanese, and existing separator behavior.

candidates.approach: Implement a comprehensive, checked-in Latin-to-ASCII lookup table rather than relying on normalization. Iterate through the lowercased title by Unicode code point, replace Latin letters with their reviewed ASCII spellings, and consume combining accents attached to Latin letters before applying the existing separator rules. Pass all other characters through unchanged. This makes transliteration decisions explicit and auditable, but requires maintaining a substantially larger table and defining coverage for uncommon Latin letters.
candidates.firstStep: Inventory Latin letters from a pinned Unicode Character Database and create a mapping fixture that records an ASCII spelling for each supported letter, including multi-character spellings.

candidates.approach: Use an existing transliteration dependency, but invoke it only on Latin-letter spans and their attached combining marks inside slugify. Keep non-Latin spans out of the dependency entirely so its broader transliteration rules cannot convert Greek, Cyrillic, Japanese, or other scripts. Retain the current lowercase and separator behavior around this adapter, and supplement or reject the dependency if its Latin coverage is incomplete. This trades custom transliteration maintenance for dependency size, compatibility, and versioning concerns.
candidates.firstStep: Inspect the project’s dependency and runtime constraints, then evaluate candidate packages against a Latin coverage fixture and verify that the adapter can isolate Latin spans without sending neighboring non-Latin text through transliteration.

candidates.approach: Build a development-time compiler for Unicode and CLDR transliteration data that emits a dependency-free, Latin-scoped sequence-rewriting matcher for slugify. Unlike a hand-maintained code-point table, generated ordered rules can handle both individual letters and decomposed sequences, with explicit overrides for the desired ASCII spellings. The generated matcher leaves non-Latin input untouched before the existing slug cleanup. This is probably excessive for a small function, but offers reproducible coverage and a systematic Unicode-update workflow.
candidates.firstStep: Prototype a generator using pinned Unicode and CLDR data, and produce a coverage report identifying Latin letters whose generated output is missing, non-ASCII, or requires a reviewed override.
